clinicalPearls: Commonest regular paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia, disproportionately affecting women, typically presenting with abrupt-onset, abrupt-offset palpitations.

Substrate is dual atrioventricular nodal physiology: a slow pathway with short refractoriness and a fast pathway with longer refractoriness, permitting a reentry circuit within or adjacent to the compact node.
Typical (slow-fast) AVNRT conducts antegradely down the slow pathway and retrogradely up the fast pathway, giving near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation.
On the surface ECG the retrograde P wave is usually buried in the QRS or produces a pseudo-r' in V1 and a pseudo-S in the inferior leads, a valuable diagnostic clue.
Vagal manoeuvres and adenosine terminate the arrhythmia by transiently blocking the AV node, distinguishing it from atrial tachycardias that continue despite block.
A neck-pounding sensation (frog sign) reflects simultaneous atrial and ventricular contraction against closed AV valves producing cannon A waves.
Atypical (fast-slow or slow-slow) variants show a long RP interval with the retrograde P separated from the QRS, mimicking atrial tachycardia or PJRT.
Catheter ablation of the slow pathway near the coronary sinus os is curative in the great majority with a low risk of inadvertent AV block.
reference.pathophysiology: AVNRT arises from functionally and anatomically distinct conduction pathways in the region of the atrioventricular node. A fast pathway conducts rapidly but has a long refractory period, whereas a slow pathway conducts slowly but recovers quickly. A critically timed atrial premature beat blocks in the fast pathway and descends the slow pathway; by the time it reaches the distal node the fast pathway has recovered, allowing retrograde conduction back to the atrium and initiation of a sustained reentrant circuit. In typical slow-fast AVNRT this produces near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular depolarisation, while atypical forms reverse or vary the pathways used. The circuit incorporates perinodal atrial tissue and does not require an accessory pathway or the ventricles for its maintenance.
additionalDifferentials: atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia using a concealed accessory pathway
additionalInvestigations: twelve-lead ECG during tachycardia and in sinus rhythm to seek pseudo-r' or pseudo-S waves
ambulatory or event monitoring to capture onset and offset if episodes are infrequent
vagal manoeuvre or adenosine administration with continuous ECG to observe response
transthoracic echocardiography to exclude structural heart disease
electrophysiological study demonstrating dual AV nodal physiology and a jump in the AH interval
thyroid function and full blood count to identify precipitants
redFlags: haemodynamic compromise with hypotension, chest pain or syncope during tachycardia
very rapid rates in patients with pre-existing coronary or structural heart disease
syncope at onset suggesting an accessory pathway or additional arrhythmia
signs of decompensated heart failure during sustained episodes
reference.prognosis: AVNRT is a benign arrhythmia with an excellent long-term prognosis and is not associated with increased mortality in structurally normal hearts. Slow-pathway catheter ablation offers a durable cure in the great majority, and episodes otherwise remain intermittent and self-limiting.
pitfalls: Mistaking the pseudo-r' in V1 for genuine incomplete right bundle branch block and overlooking retrograde atrial activation.
Assuming failure of adenosine to terminate excludes a nodal-dependent arrhythmia when subtherapeutic dosing or rapid metabolism is the cause.
Labelling atypical long-RP AVNRT as atrial tachycardia and choosing an inappropriate ablation target.
Attributing palpitations to anxiety in young women and delaying definitive rhythm documentation.
Overlooking coexisting dual pathophysiology when AVNRT and an accessory pathway occur in the same patient.
